(Lataifah)

Reflect on the surahs that begin with single letters, and you will find that the surah is built upon the word of that letter. Thus, for (Qaf), the surah is built upon words containing the letter qaf: the mention of the Qur'an, the mention of creation, the repetition and reconsideration of speech again and again, the nearness to the son of Adam, the two angels receiving the servant's words, the mention of the Watcher, the mention of the driver and the companion, the casting into Hellfire, the advance warning of punishment, the mention of the God-fearing, the mention of the heart, the generations, and the traversing of lands, the mention of the saying repeated twice, the splitting of the earth, the casting of firm mountains into it, the towering palm trees and provision, the mention of peoples and the realization of the threat, and it would suffice if there were nothing but the repetition of speech and dialogue. There is another secret: that all the meanings of this surah correspond to the qualities of the letter qaf, which are strength, voicing, height, and openness.

(Section)

This surah has gathered from the foundations of faith what suffices, heals, and makes one independent of the speculation of the people of kalam (scholastic theology) and the rational arguments of the people of reason (ma'qul).

For it includes the affirmation of the origin (mabda'), the return (ma'ad), monotheism (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwah), faith in the angels, and the division of people into the ruined wretched and the successful happy, along with the attributes of both groups. It includes the affirmation of God's attributes of perfection and His transcendence above whatever contradicts His perfection of deficiencies and defects. It mentions in it the lesser resurrection and the greater resurrection, and the greater world, which is the world of the Hereafter, and the lesser world, which is the world of this life. It mentions in it the creation of man, his death, his re-creation, his state at death, and the day of his return, and God's encompassing of him from every aspect, to the extent that He knows the whisperings of his soul, and the establishment of the guardians over him, who count every word he utters, and that he will be met on the Day of Resurrection with a driver who drives him to Him and a witness who testifies against him. When the driver brings him, he says: ﴿This is what is ready with me.﴾

That is, "This is the one whom You commanded to be brought, and I have brought him." Then, when he is brought, it is said: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾, just as a criminal is brought into the presence of the ruler, and it is said, "This is so-and-so, I have brought him," and he says, "Take him to the prison and punish him as he deserves."

Consider how the surah explicitly indicates that God will restore this very body which obeyed and disobeyed, and will bless and punish it, just as He blesses the soul that believed in its very self and punishes the soul that disbelieved in its very self. It is not that He creates another soul other than this one and blesses and punishes it, as said by one who did not know the return that the messengers informed of, when he claimed that God creates a body other than this body in every respect, upon which blessing and punishment fall, and that the soul is, in his view, an accident of the body, so He creates a soul other than this soul and a body other than this body. This is not what the messengers agreed upon, and what the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and all the books of God indicate. In reality, this is a denial of the return and an agreement with the one who denied it among the deniers, for they did not deny God's power to create other bodies other than these bodies to punish and bless. How could they, when they witness the human species creating one thing after another? At every moment God creates bodies and souls other than the bodies that have perished. So how do they marvel at something they witness with their own eyes? They only marvelled at their return in their very selves after decay had torn them apart and they had become bones and crumbled dust. They marvelled that they themselves, in their very selves, would be raised for recompense. For this reason they said: ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?﴾

And they said: ﴿That is a far-off return.﴾ If the recompense were only for bodies other than these, that would not be a resurrection or a return, but rather a beginning, and His saying ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ would have no great meaning. For He, glory be to Him, made this an answer to a presumed question, namely that He distinguishes those parts that mixed with the earth and turned into elements in such a way that they cannot be distinguished.

So He informed that He knows what the earth consumes of their flesh, bones, and hair, and that just as He is knowing of those parts, He is able to gather them together after their dispersal and assemble them into a new creation. He, glory be to Him, establishes the return by mentioning His perfect knowledge, His perfect power, and His perfect wisdom. The doubts of those who deny it all return to three types. The first is that their parts mix with the parts of the earth in a way that cannot be distinguished, and no distinction of one person from another can be achieved. The second is that power does not relate to that. The third is that this is a matter of no benefit, or that wisdom only required the continuance of the human species one after another forever, so that whenever one generation dies another succeeds it. But that He should cause the entire human species to die and then revive it afterward has no wisdom in it. So the proofs of the return in the Qur'an come upon three foundations. The first is the affirmation of the perfect knowledge of the Lord, glory be to Him, as He said in answer to one who ﴿said, "Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?" Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knower of all creation."﴾

And He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming, so forgive with gracious forgiveness. Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the All-Knowing.﴾ And He said: ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them.﴾

The second is the affirmation of His perfect power, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ and His saying: ﴿Yes, [We are] able to even restore his fingertips.﴾ and His saying: ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent.﴾

He, glory be to Him, combines both matters, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, and He is the Creator, the All-Knowing.﴾

The third is His perfect wisdom, as in His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ And His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them without purpose.﴾ And His saying: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾

And His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?  Exalted is God, the King, the Truth.﴾

And His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, [that] their living and their dying are equal? Evil is what they judge.﴾

For this reason, the correct view is that the return is known by reason along with revelation, and that the perfection of the Lord, the perfection of His names and attributes, requires it and necessitates it, and that He is transcendent above what its deniers say, just as His perfection is transcendent above all other defects and deficiencies. Then God informed that those who deny this, when they denied the truth, their affair became confused: ﴿so they are in a confused matter﴾, mixed up, and gain nothing from it. Then He called them to reflect upon the upper world, its construction, its elevation, its evenness, its beauty, and its harmony, then to the lower world, which is the earth, and how He spread it out and prepared it by spreading to suit what is intended from it, and fixed it with mountains, and deposited in it benefits, and caused to grow in it every fine kind of vegetation in its varied forms, colors, quantities, benefits, and qualities. This is a insight for the penitent servant who reflects and, by it, takes heed of what the messengers informed of, of monotheism and the return.

The one who looks at them gains insight first, then remembers second, and this is attained only by a servant who turns to God with his heart and limbs. Then He called them to reflect upon the source of their provisions, sustenance, clothing, mounts, and gardens, which is the water that He sent down from the sky and blessed, so that by it He caused gardens of varied fruits to grow, of white, black, red, and yellow, sweet and sour, and what lies between these, with varied sources and diverse kinds. By it He caused all grains to grow in their variety, their differing benefits, qualities, shapes, and quantities. Then He singled out the palm tree for what it contains of the place of lesson and sign that is not hidden from the reflecting one. By it He revived the earth after its death. Then He said: ﴿Thus will be the coming out﴾, that is, like this bringing forth from the earth of fruits, produce, sustenance, and grains, will be your coming out from the earth after you have been buried in it. We have mentioned this analogy and its like, among the analogies in the Qur'an, in our book al-Ma'alim, and explained some of the secrets and lessons in it. Then He, glory be to Him, moved to the affirmation of prophethood in the finest affirmation, with the clearest expression and the furthest from every doubt and suspicion. He informed that He sent messengers to the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot, and the people of Pharaoh, and they denied them, so He destroyed them with various kinds of destruction, and He fulfilled His threat that His messengers had warned them of, if they did not believe. This is an affirmation of their prophethood and of the prophethood of the one who informed of these matters, without having learned them from a teacher or read them in a book. Rather, he informed of them with a detailed account that matches what is with the People of the Book. The only objection to this is the question of slander and obstinacy, denying what is necessarily known, by claiming that none of that happened, or that the calamities of time and its misfortunes struck them as they struck others. The one who raises this objection knows within himself that he is a liar and a denier of what eyewitness testimony attested to and what has been transmitted generation after generation. His denial is like denying the existence of famous kings, scholars, and distant lands. Then He, glory be to Him, returned to affirming the return by His saying: ﴿Were We then fatigued by the first creation?﴾

It is said of anyone who is unable to do something: "He was 'ayiya (unable) to it," and "So-and-so was unable (ʿiya) with this matter."

The poet said:
"They were unable with their affair, as the dove was unable with its egg."

And from this is His saying: ﴿And He was not fatigued by their creation.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: he means, "Were We unable?" And likewise Muqatil said. I say: this is an explanation by a necessary implication of the word, but its true meaning is more general than that. For the Arabs say, "I was unable (a'yani) to know such-and-such," and "I was unable (ʿiyītu) with it," when you were not guided to its way and were unable to know or attain it. So they say, "Your medicine was unable (a'yani) for me," when you were not guided to it and did not come to know it. The necessary implication of this meaning is inability regarding it. The verse of poetry they cited as evidence supports this meaning, for the dove is not unable with her egg. Rather, when she wants to lay, she is unable to know where to drop the egg, so she circles and wanders until she drops it. Then, once she has laid it, she is unable to know where to guard and hide it so that it cannot be reached. So she moves it from place to place and is confused about where to make her resting place, just as is the state of one who is unable with his affair, not knowing from where to approach it or from where it will come to him. The meaning of fatigue (i'a') in this verse is not weariness, as one who does not know the interpretation of the Qur'an supposes. Rather, this is the meaning that He negated of Himself at the end of the surah in His saying: ﴿And no weariness touched Us.﴾

Then God informed that they are ﴿in doubt about a new creation﴾, that is, they were confused about the re-creation of creation anew. Then He alerted them to what is among the greatest signs of His power, the evidences of His lordship, and the proofs of the return: the creation of man. For it is among the greatest proofs of monotheism and the return. What proof is clearer than the composition of this human form, with its limbs, powers, and attributes, and what it contains of flesh, bone, veins, nerves, ligaments, passages, instruments, knowledge, wills, and crafts, all of it from a drop of water? If the servant were just to his Lord, he would be content with reflecting on himself and would infer, from his own existence, all that the messengers informed of concerning God, His names, and His attributes. Then God informed of the encompassing of His knowledge over him, to the extent that He knows the whisperings of his soul, and then informed of His nearness to him through knowledge and encompassment, and that this is nearer to him than the vein that is within his body. So He is nearer to him by power over him and knowledge of him than that vein. My teacher said: the meaning of "We" in His saying is His angels, as He said: ﴿So when We recite it, follow its recitation﴾, that is, when Our messenger Gabriel recites it to you. He said: and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿when the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left.﴾ So the nearness mentioned is restricted by the time of the two angels' reception. Had the intended meaning been nearness of essence, it would not have been restricted to the time of the reception of the two angels. Thus the verse supports neither the incarnationist nor the one who negates attributes.

Then God informed that on his right and his left are two angels who record his deeds and his words. By counting the words and writing them down, He alerted to the recording of deeds, which occur less frequently than words and have greater effect, and which are the ends and final results of words. Then He informed of the lesser resurrection, which is the agony of death, and that it comes with truth, which is the meeting with Him, the arrival before Him, the presentation of the soul before Him, and the reward and punishment that are hastened for it before the greater resurrection.

Then He mentioned the greater resurrection in His saying: ﴿And the Horn is blown; that is the Day of the Threat.﴾

Then He informed of the states of creation on this day, that every person comes to God, glory be to Him, on that day with a driver who drives him and a witness who testifies against him. This is other than the testimony of his limbs, other than the testimony of the earth on which he stood against him, other than the testimony of His messenger and the believers. For God, glory be to Him, calls upon the guardians, the prophets, and the places where they did good and evil, and the skins with which they disobeyed Him, as witnesses against the servant. He does not judge between them by His bare knowledge, and He is the most just of judges and the most wise of rulers.

For this reason, He informed His prophet that He judges between people by what He hears of their confession and the testimony of evidence, not by His bare knowledge alone. How then is it permissible for a judge to judge by his bare knowledge without evidence or confession?

Then God informed, glory be to Him, that man is in heedlessness of this matter, which deserves that he should not be heedless of it, and that he should never cease to remember it and its consequences, and He said: ﴿You were in heedlessness of this.﴾

He did not say "of it" (ʿanhu), as He said: ﴿And indeed they are in doubt about it, suspicious.﴾ and He did not say "in doubt concerning it." This came in the verbal noun (maṣdar) though it did not come in the verb, for one does not say "ghafilt minhu" (I was heedless from it) or "shakakt minhu" (I doubted from it). It is as if his heedlessness and doubt originated from it. So it is the origin of his heedlessness and doubt. This is more eloquent than saying "in heedlessness of it" and "in doubt concerning it," for He made what should be the origin of reminder and certainty and their source into an origin of heedlessness and doubt.

Then He informed that the covering of heedlessness and stupor will be removed on that day, as the covering of sleep is removed from the heart so that it awakens, and from the eye so that it opens. So the relation of removing this covering from the servant at the moment of witnessing is like the relation of removing the covering of sleep from him at the moment of waking.

Then God informed, glory be to Him, that his companion, who was paired with him in this world from among the angels, records his deeds, and his speech says, when he is brought: "This is what you appointed me to, in this world. I have brought him and come to you with him." This is the statement of Mujahid. Ibn Qutaybah said the meaning is: "This is what I wrote against him and counted of his words and deeds, present with me." The verification is that the verse includes both meanings: this is the person you appointed me over, and this is his deed that I counted against him. Then it is said: ﴿Cast into Hell.﴾

This is one of the two possibilities regarding the address: it is either addressed to the driver and the witness, or to the angel charged with punishing him. Although it is singular, this is a well-known style among the Arabs in their address. Or the alif may be a transformation of the light emphatic nun (nun al-ta'kid al-khafifah), with the pause treated as continuation (wasl given the status of waqf).

Then He mentioned the attributes of this one who is cast into the Fire. He mentioned six attributes for him:

The first: he is ungrateful for the favours of Allah and His rights, ungrateful toward His religion, His tawhid, His names and His attributes, ungrateful toward His messengers and His angels, and ungrateful toward His books and His meeting.

The second: he opposes the truth, repelling it out of denial and obstinacy.

The third: he withholds good (mannaʿ lil-khayr). This encompasses his withholding of the good that is a benefit to himself, such as acts of obedience and nearness to Allah, and the good that is a benefit to people. There is no good in him for himself or for his fellow human beings, as is the case with most of creation.

The fourth: despite his withholding of good, he transgresses against people, is oppressive and tyrannical, transgressing against them with his hand and his tongue.

The fifth: he is murib, meaning one who has doubt and suspicion. Along with this, he is prone to every doubt. It is said, "So-and-so is murib" when he is a person of doubt.

The sixth: despite all this, he is a polytheist (mushrik) with Allah. He has taken another god alongside Allah, which he worships, loves, becomes angry for, is pleased for, swears by its name, vows for, allies himself for, and is hostile for. Thus he and his companion from among the devils dispute, and he refers the matter to Him, saying that it was his companion who made him rebellious and led him astray. His companion says: "I had no power to make him go astray or to make him rebellious, but he was in far error. He chose it for himself and preferred it over the truth," just as Iblis said to the people of the Fire: ﴿And I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me﴾. Accordingly, the companion here is his devil, and the two dispute before Allah.

A group said: rather, his companion here is the angel. He claims against him that he added to what was recorded against him, that he transgressed, that he did not do all of that, and that he hurried him in the recording before repentance and did not give him time to repent. The angel says: "I did not add to the recording beyond what he did, nor did I hasten him away from repentance." ﴿But he was in far error﴾. Then the Lord, exalted is He, says: ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾.

Allah, glorified is He, has informed us of the dispute of the disbelievers and the devils before Him in Surat al-Saffat and Surat al-A'raf.

He informed us of the dispute of people before Him in Surat al-Zumar, and He informed us of the dispute of the people of the Fire within it in Surat al-Shu'ara' and Surat Sad.

Then He, glorified is He, informed that the word is not changed in His presence. It was said that what is meant by this is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together﴾, and His promise to the people of faith of Paradise, and that this is not altered or broken.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He means: what is promised will not be changed for the people of My obedience nor for the people of My disobedience."

Mujahid said: "I have decreed what I am the decreer of."

This is the more correct of the two views regarding the verse.

There is another view: that the meaning is that the word is not altered before Me by falsehood and deception, as it is altered before kings and rulers. Thus the word here refers to the speech of the disputants. This is the view chosen by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Farra' said: "The meaning is that it is not falsified before Me, because of My knowledge of the unseen." Ibn Qutaybah said: "That is, the word is not distorted before Me, nor is anything added to it or subtracted from it." He said: "Because He said al-qawl ʿindi (the word before Me) and did not say qawli (My word), and this is like the saying 'it is not lied to before me'."

According to the first view, His saying ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾ is part of His saying ﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾, meaning: what I have said and promised must certainly be carried out. Yet, along with this, it is just and contains no injustice or tyranny.

According to the second view, He has described Himself with two matters:

One: the perfection of His knowledge and awareness prevents the alteration of speech before Him and the promotion of falsehood upon Him. The perfection of His justice and His independence prevents His wronging His servants.

Then He informed of the vastness of Hell and that whenever things are cast into it, it says: ﴿Is there any more?﴾ Whoever said that this is in the sense of negation, meaning "there is no more," has erred, and the authentic hadith refutes this interpretation.

Then He informed of the nearness of Paradise to the God-fearing, and that its people are those who possess these four attributes:

The first: that they be awwab, meaning those who return to Allah from disobedience to obedience, and from heedlessness of Him to remembrance of Him.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: "The awwab is the one who remembers his sins and then seeks forgiveness for them."

Mujahid said: "He is the one who, when he remembers his sin in private, seeks forgiveness for it."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "He is the one who sins, then repents, then sins, then repents."

The second: that they be hafiz (guardians).

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Guarding what Allah has entrusted to him and enjoined upon him."

Qatadah said: "One who guards what Allah has entrusted to him of His right and His blessing."

Since the soul has two powers, the power of seeking and the power of restraint, the awwab employs the power of seeking in his return to Allah, His good pleasure and His obedience, while the hafiz employs the power of guarding in restraining himself from His disobedience and prohibitions. So the hafiz is one who restrains himself from what has been forbidden to him, and the awwab is one who turns toward Allah in obedience.

The third: His saying ﴿who feared the Most Merciful unseen﴾.

This includes affirming His existence, His lordship, His power, His knowledge, and His awareness of the details of the servant's circumstances. It includes affirming His books, His messengers, His command and His prohibition, and it includes affirming His promise, His threat and the meeting with Him. The fear of the Most Merciful in the unseen is not valid except after all of this.

The fourth: His saying ﴿and came with a heart turned in repentance﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "One who returns from the disobedience of Allah and turns toward the obedience of Allah." The reality of inābah (turning in repentance) is the heart's devotion to the obedience of Allah, its love of Him, and its turning toward Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the reward of those in whom these attributes are present, in His saying: ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity. For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more.﴾ Then He warned them that there would befall them the destruction that befell those before them, and that they were stronger than them in might, yet the severity of their might did not avert destruction from them. At the time of destruction they turned about and traveled through the lands: ﴿Is there any place of escape?﴾ — any refuge from the punishment of Allah. Qatadah said: "The enemies of Allah sought refuge and found the command of Allah overtaking them." Al-Zajjaj said: "They roamed and searched, but found no escape from death."

The reality of this is that they sought a means of escape from death and did not find it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that in what has been mentioned there is a reminder ﴿for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness.﴾

Then He informed that He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness or fatigue touched Him.

This is a refutation of His enemies among the Jews, who said that He rested on the seventh day.

Then He commanded His Prophet to emulate Him, glorified is He, in patience over what His enemies say about Him, just as He, glorified is He, was patient with the Jews' saying that He rested. No one is more patient over harm heard from them than Him.

Then He commanded him with what would help him in patience, which is glorifying the praise of his Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and at night and at the adbar of prostrations. It was said that this refers to the witr prayer. It was also said that it refers to the two rak'ahs after maghrib.

The first is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, and the second is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAli, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan ibn ʿAli, and one of the two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbas.

A third narration from Ibn ʿAbbas: it is glorification with the tongue after the obligatory prayers (adbar al-salah al-maktubat).

Then He concluded the surah by mentioning the Return and the call of the caller to the return of souls to their bodies for the gathering.

He informed that this call comes from a near place, which everyone will hear: ﴿On the Day they hear the Cry in truth﴾ — the resurrection and the meeting with Allah — ﴿the Day the earth will split open from them, as it splits open over vegetation, and they will come out hastening. That is a gathering easy for Him.﴾ Then He, glorified is He, informed that He knows what His enemies say, and this implies His recompense for them for their words, since nothing is hidden from Him. He, glorified is He, mentions His knowledge and power to establish the recompense. Then He informed him that He has no authority over them and is not a compeller, and that He was not sent to force them into Islam or compel them to it. He commanded him to remind by His speech whoever fears His threat, for it is he who benefits from the reminder.

As for one who does not believe in meeting Him, does not fear His threat, and does not hope for His reward, he does not benefit from the reminder.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 50, verses 6–8:

He said, regarding His witnessed signs: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts? And the earth—We spread it out and cast into it firm mountains, and We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair—an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back (to Allah).﴾

So the tabsirah (insight) is the instrument of sight, and the tadhkirah (reminder) is the instrument of remembrance. He joined them together and made them for the people of inábah (turning back to Allah), because when the servant turns back to Allah, he sees the places of the signs and the lessons, and so he draws evidence from them that they are signs pointing to Him. Thereby aversion is removed from him through turning back, blindness through insight, and heedlessness through remembrance, because insight makes the form of the signified object arise in the heart after his heedlessness of it. Thus the arrangement of the three stations is the best arrangement. Moreover, each of them supports its companion, strengthens it, and makes it bear fruit.

And he said in (Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back﴾.

So the tabsirah is intellection (ta'aqqul), and the tadhkirah is recollection (tadhakkur), and reflection (fikr) is the gate to them and their entrance. So when one reflects, one gains insight. And when one gains insight, one recollects.

The reminder in the verse came in its arrangement upon the intellect, which is arranged upon reflection. So reflection is placed first, as it is the gate and the entrance, and intellect is placed in the middle, as it is the fruit and result of reflection, and recollection is placed last, as it is what is sought from reflection and intellect. So reflect upon this with the deepest reflection.

And the earth—We spread it out and cast into it firm mountains, and We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair—an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back (to Allah).﴾

So the tabsirah (insight) is the instrument of sight, and the tadhkirah (reminder) is the instrument of remembrance. He joined them together and made them for the people of inábah (turning back to Allah), because when the servant turns back to Allah, he sees the places of the signs and the lessons, and so he draws evidence from them that they are signs pointing to Him. Thereby aversion is removed from him through turning back, blindness through insight, and heedlessness through remembrance, because insight makes the form of the signified object arise in the heart after his heedlessness of it. Thus the arrangement of the three stations is the best arrangement. Moreover, each of them supports its companion, strengthens it, and makes it bear fruit.

And he said in (Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back﴾.

So the tabsirah is intellection (ta'aqqul), and the tadhkirah is recollection (tadhakkur), and reflection (fikr) is the gate to them and their entrance. So when one reflects, one gains insight. And when one gains insight, one recollects.

The reminder in the verse came in its arrangement upon the intellect, which is arranged upon reflection. So reflection is placed first, as it is the gate and the entrance, and intellect is placed in the middle, as it is the fruit and result of reflection, and recollection is placed last, as it is what is sought from reflection and intellect. So reflect upon this with the deepest reflection.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 50, verse 10:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And palm trees with spathes of fruit hanging close together﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:148].

Tal'u al-nakhl (the spathe of the date palm): what appears of its fruit at the first emergence of its blossom. Its sheath is called al-Kufurra. Al-Nadid (the close-packed) is that which is arranged one upon another in layers; it is called nadid only so long as it is still within its kufurra. Once it has opened, it is no longer nadid.

As for al-Hadim, it is that whose parts are pressed together one against another, so it is likewise close-packed, and this occurs before the kufurra splits open around it.

The tal' (spathe) is of two kinds: male and female. Pollination (al-talqih) is that one takes from the male, which is like fine wheat flour, and places it in the female; this is al-ta'bir, and it is the equivalent of fertilisation between the male and the female. Muslim has related in his Sahih, from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among palm trees, and he saw some people pollinating, and he said: 'What are these people doing?' They said: 'They take from the male and place it in the female.' He said: 'I do not think that this benefits anything.' When this reached them, they left it off, and the crop was poor. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is only a supposition. If it benefits them, then do it, for I am only a human being like you, and supposition may be right or wrong. But what I tell you from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, I will not lie about Allah.'" End of quotation.

(Benefit)

The spathe of the date palm is beneficial for sexual vigour and increases intercourse. Its fine pollen, if a woman takes it before intercourse, greatly aids conception. It is in the second degree of coldness and dryness; it strengthens the stomach and dries it, and calms the agitation of the blood, together with thickness and slow digestion.

It is tolerated only by those of hot temperament. Whoever consumes much of it should take with it some hot digestive confections (al-jawarishat al-harara). It binds the nature and strengthens the viscera. The heart of the palm (al-jummar) is similar to it, as are the unripe dates (al-balah) and the semi-ripe dates (al-busr). Excessive consumption of it harms the stomach and chest and may occasionally cause colic (al-qawlanj); its remedy is with clarified butter (al-samn) or with what has been mentioned before.

(The Secrets of the Rules of Pronouns)

The pronouns in their speech number about sixty, and their states are well known, but we will draw attention to their secrets.

(On the Rules of Pronouns)

Know that when the speaker dispensed with the apparent noun in the context of speech, because the presence (of the referent) indicates it, he placed in its stead a word that points to it. That word is composed of a hamzah and a nun. As for the hamzah, its point of articulation is from the chest, which is the closest place of the voice to the speaker, since the speaker in reality is located behind the jugular vein. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾. Do you not see Him saying: ﴿Not a word does he utter except that with him is an observer ready﴾?

That is, what the speaker utters, which shows that the speaker is closest to the jugular vein. So when the speaker in reality is located there, and you want from the letters one that expresses him, the most fitting of them is the one whose articulation comes from his direction and the nearest places to his location, and there is none but the hamzah or the haa'. The hamzah is more deserving of the speaker because of its strength through being voiced and firm, while the haa' is weak through being hidden. So what is more voiced is stronger and more fitting to express the name of the speaker, of which speech is an attribute, and he is more entitled to be described by it.

As for its being joined with the haa' together with the nun: since the hamzah, when standing alone, cannot be a separate noun, it was more fitting for the nun to be joined to it, or a letter of prolongation and softness, since they are the mothers of the augmentations. Letters of prolongation could not be combined with the hamzah because they would disappear when two consonants meet, as in: ana al-rajul (I am the man).

Had the second letter been dropped, the hamzah would remain alone in most speech with the definite article lam, and it would be confused with the alif, which is the sister of the lam, and most speech would be disordered.

So the most fitting thing to attach to it was the nun, because of its nearness to the letter of prolongation and softness. Then they fixed the nun because of its hiddenness, with an alif in the state of pause, or with a haa' in the dialect of one who says (innih). Then, since the addressee shares with the speaker in the state of the meaning of speech, for speech begins with the speaker and ends at the addressee, and were it not for the addressee, the speaker's speech would not be an audible word nor need to be expressed, when the two shared in the purpose of speech and its benefit, they shared in the word that signifies the apparent noun, which is the alif and the nun, and they were distinguished from each other by the taa' alone, and the taa' was specified for the addressee because it is established as the mark of the pronoun in (qumta).

If you say: it is the mark of the speaker's pronoun in (qumtu), so why was the addressee more entitled to it?

I say: the original of the taa' is for the addressee, and the speaker is an intruder upon it. Since it was an intruder upon it, they specified it with the damma, because in it there is what there is of plurality and an indication to oneself that is not in the fatha.

And they specified the addressee with the fatha, because in the fatha there is an indication toward him that is not in the damma.

And this is known by sense.

As for the speaker's pronoun in the genitive, it was (ya') because when the apparent noun was left in its wording through dispensing, and there was no escape from a sign indicating it, the most fitting letter for that was a letter of the pronoun-noun, and that is not possible because the names of speakers differ. What they intended was a sign specific to each speaker in the genitive state, and nouns differ in their wording but agree in the state of annexation to the ya' in the kasra, which is the sign of the genitive. However, the kasra does not stand by itself until it becomes a ya', so they made the (ya') a sign for every speaker in the genitive. Then they made the accusative share with it in the form of the pronoun, because they are equal in meaning, except that they added a nun to the accusative pronoun as a protection for the verb from the kasra.

As for the attached speaker's pronoun in the nominative, its sign is the damma taa'.

As for the plural speakers, their sign is (na) in all states. Its secret is that when they left the apparent noun and wanted from the letters one that would be a sign for it, they took from the apparent noun what all speakers share in the state of plurality and duality, which is the nun at the end of the word, found in the dual and plural in the nominative, accusative and genitive. So they made it a sign for speakers, whether plural or dual, and they added after it an alif, lest it resemble the tanwin or the light nun.

And for another wisdom, which is nearness to the word (anā), since it is from the pronouns of the speakers, for it is a speaker's pronoun. Nothing was dropped from the word anā except the hamzah, which is the origin for the singular speaker.

As for the plural speaker and its dual, it is a branch that flew away from the origin, so the hamzah, whose specificity to the speaker was established earlier, could not be in it, until it was specified to it in (af'alu).

And the addressee was specified with the taa' in (taf'alu) for what we have mentioned.

As for the attached nominative pronoun, it was specified with the (taa') only because when they wanted a letter that would be a sign for the apparent noun dispensed with mentioning it, the most fitting letter for that was a letter from the noun, which varies, as has preceded. So they took from the noun what nouns do not differ in, in the nominative state, which is the damma. The damma does not stand by itself unless it is a waw. Then they saw that the waw cannot receive the vowel changes because of its heaviness, while they need vowels in this pronoun to distinguish the speaker, the feminine addressee and the masculine addressee. So they made the (taa') in place of the (waw), because of its nearness to its point of articulation, and because it is often replaced by it in much speech, as in (turath and tujah). So the speaker's and addressee's pronouns shared the taa', just as they shared the alif and nun in (anā and anta), because they are partners in speech: since speech belongs to the addressee it is a word, and since it belongs to the speaker it is a meaning.

Then the distinction between their two pronouns came about by the vowel rather than the letter, for the reason already stated.

As for the addressee's pronoun in the accusative and genitive, it was the kaf rather than the ya', because the ya' has been specified to the speaker in the accusative and genitive. Had the vowels been established in it, or had there been something to stand in its place in the substitution as the taa' was with the waw, the addressee would have shared with the speaker in the genitive state, as he shared with him in the rest in the nominative state. Since that was not the case, and there was no escape from letters that would be a sign of the pronoun, the kaf was more entitled to this position, because addressees, though their apparent nouns differ, each of them is a speaker, and his aim in speech, which is the wording, and for whose sake the wording is needed to express what is in the soul, is the speech. So the speech that begins with it in the wording of speech became the sign of the addressee's pronoun.

Do you not see that it is only a sign of the pronoun for him after a speech, like the verb and the subject, as in (akramtuka, I honored you), because they are a speech, and the verb alone is not a speech. Therefore the kaf is not a sign of the pronoun except after a speech of verb and subject, or subject and predicate.

If it is said: the speaker is also the owner of the speech, so he is more entitled that the kaf taken from the word of speech be the sign of the noun?

It is said: the kaf is a word, so it is more entitled to the addressee, because speech is only uttered on his account.

As for the detached pronoun of the absent third person, it is haa' followed by waw. Because the absent is mentioned in the heart and dispensed with its apparent noun by its prior mention, the haa', whose point of articulation is from the chest near the place of mention, was more fitting to be an expression of

what is mentioned in the heart. The hamzah was not used, because it is voiced and firm, so it was more fitting for the speaker, who is more apparent. The haa', for its hiddenness, is more fitting for the absent, who is more hidden and inward. Then it was joined with the waw, because it is a word by which one signals to the addressee so that what is in the soul of the mentioned is known, and signalling is with the lips, and the waw's point of articulation is from there, so it was specified with that.

Then they extended their principle to the pronoun of the singular absent, making it haa' in all its states except the nominative. They did this because they saw the distinction between the states arising from the change of the pronoun's form. When the genitive particle enters upon it, the haa' is kasra and its waw becomes ya'. When it does not enter, it remains damma as its origin. When in the nominative state it has no sign in the wording, because the apparent noun before the verb is a clear marker that makes the addressee needless of a sign of the pronoun in the verb, unlike the speaker and addressee. For you say about the absent: (Zayd is standing), and you find the noun to which the pronoun returns present and apparent in the wording. But you do not say about the speaker (Zayd I stood) or about the addressee (Zayd you stood).

Since the states of the absent pronoun differed, through the loss of its sign in the nominative and the change of the haa' by the entry of genitive particles, that was for them in place of the signs of inflection in the apparent noun, and is in the pronoun like them, such as the taa' substituted for the waw, the ya' established, the kasra, and the kaf specified to the object and genitive following a complete speech. Nothing follows a speech except an accusative or genitive, so the kaf taken from the word of speech was the sign of the accusative and genitive when the addressee is meant.

As for (naḥnu), it is the detached pronoun of the speakers, dual and plural. It was specified with this because they could not form the dual and plural of the speaking pronoun, since the reality of the dual is joining one thing to a like of it in wording, and the plural is joining one thing to more than it of a like in wording.

So when you say (Zaydān), its meaning is Zayd and Zayd, and (antum) means you and you. The speaker cannot bring a dual or plural noun in meaning, because he cannot say (anā) and join to himself a like of it in wording. Since that was impossible, and there was no escape from a word indicating that meaning, even if he is not so in reality, they brought a word that applies to the dual and the plural in this place. Then the word ended with a nun, and at its beginning there is an indication to the earlier original which they could not bring, namely the dual of (anā), which is like the wording being joined to its like. So when they could not do that in a dual wording, the repeated nun was a reminder and an allusion to it. The nun was specified for this rather than the hamzah, for the reason mentioned before, that the plural pronoun is specified with the nun and the speaker's pronoun with the hamzah. Then they placed between the nuns a quiescent ḥā', because of its nearness to the point of articulation of the alif found in the speaker's pronoun before and after the nun. Then they built it on the damma rather than the fatha or kasra, indicating that it is a nominative pronoun. The evidence for this is what we have said in the chapter about the indication of the disjointed letters on meanings and their pointing to them.

(Gathering the left sides in the plural and keeping the right side in the singular)

Likewise, its occurrence in the singular in His saying: ﴿Seated on the right and on the left.﴾

Since the intended meaning is that each servant has two attendants, one seated on his right and one on his left, who record for him the good and the bad, each servant has specific angels assigned to his right and his left from among the guardians. So there is no sense in using the plural here. This is unlike the saying of the Exalted, relating from Iblis: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left.﴾

Here the plural is in correspondence with the multitude of people he intends to lead astray, as if he swore that he would come to each one of them from before him, from behind him, from his right and from his left.

It would not be appropriate here to say "from their right and from their left" (in the singular), rather the plural here corresponds to the whole with the whole, which requires distributing the individuals.

**Section: Speech (al-lafzah)**

As for speech, guarding it means that a person does not utter a wasted word. He should speak only about what he hopes will bring him profit and an increase in his religion. When he wants to say something, he should consider whether it contains any benefit. If it has none, he refrains from it. If it does have benefit, he considers whether a better word would be missed by saying it, and if so, he does not waste his speech on it. And if you want to infer what is in the heart, infer it from the movement of the tongue, for it reveals to you what is in the heart, whether its owner wishes or not.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "Hearts are like cooking pots boiling with what is in them, and tongues are their ladles. So look at a man when he speaks, for his tongue scoops up for you what is in his heart: sweet, sour, fresh, bitter, and other things. The scooping of his tongue shows you the taste of his heart, just as you taste with your tongue the taste of the food in the pots and so come to know its reality. In the same way, you taste what is in a man's heart through his tongue, and you savour what is in his heart through his tongue, just as you savour what is in the pot with your tongue."

In the marfu' hadith of Anas:

"The faith of a servant is not upright until his heart is upright, and his heart is not upright until his tongue is upright."

"The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about what most causes people to enter the Fire, and he said: 'The mouth and the private parts.'"

Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

Mu'adh asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the deed that would admit him to Paradise and keep him far from the Fire. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed him of its head, its pillar, and the peak of its hump. Then he said: "Shall I not tell you the foundation of all that?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." So he took hold of his own tongue and said: "Restrain this." Mu'adh said: "Will we be held accountable for what we say?" He said: "May your mother be bereft of you, O Mu'adh! Will people be thrown on their faces, or on their noses, into the Fire for anything other than the harvest of their tongues?"

Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

It is strange that a person finds it easy to guard himself and to abstain from eating what is unlawful, from oppression, adultery, theft, drinking wine, and forbidden gazing, and other things, yet finds it hard to guard the movement of his tongue. You may see a man pointed to for his religiosity, asceticism and worship, who utters words that anger Allah without giving them a second thought, and one such word may take him further than the distance between the East and the West. And how often you see a man who abstains from indecency and oppression, yet his tongue tears into the honour of the living and the dead, and he does not care what he says.

If you want to know this, consider what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"A man said: 'By Allah, Allah will never forgive so-and-so.' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Who is this who swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? I have forgiven him, and I have nullified your deeds.'"

This worshipper, who worshipped Allah as much as he wished, had all his deeds nullified by this single word.

In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah there is something similar. Then Abu Hurayrah said: "He spoke a word that destroyed his worldly life and his Hereafter."

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"A servant may speak a word that pleases Allah, giving it no thought, and Allah raises him by it in degrees. And a servant may speak a word that angers Allah, giving it no thought, and he falls by it into the Fire of Hell."

In Muslim's version: "A servant may speak a word without clarifying its meaning, and by it he slips into the Fire further than the distance between the East and the West."

In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Bilal ibn al-Harith al-Muzani, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"One of you may speak a word that pleases Allah, not thinking it will reach as far as it does, and Allah writes His pleasure for him by it until the Day he meets Him. And one of you may speak a word that angers Allah, not thinking it will reach as far as it does, and Allah writes His anger for him by it until the Day he meets Him."

Alqamah used to say: "How many a speech has the hadith of Bilal ibn al-Harith kept me from!"

Also in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Anas, who said:

"A man from among the Companions died, and a man said: 'Good news: Paradise!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'How do you know? Perhaps he spoke about what did not concern him, or withheld what would not have harmed him.'"

He said: "A hasan hadith."

In another version: "A boy was martyred on the day of Uhud, and a stone was found tied to his stomach because of hunger. His mother wiped the dust from his face and said: 'Congratulations to you, my son, on Paradise!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'How do you know? Perhaps he used to speak about what did not concern him, and withhold what did not harm him.'"

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or keep silent."

In a version of Muslim: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, when he witnesses a matter, let him speak good or be silent."

Al-Tirmidhi also mentioned, with a sahih chain, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Part of the goodness of a person's Islam is leaving what does not concern him."

From Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying in Islam about which I will not ask anyone after you.' He said: 'Say: I believe in Allah, then be upright.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you fear most for me?' He took hold of his own tongue and said: 'This.'"

The hadith is sahih.

From Umm Habibah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"Every speech of the son of Adam is against him and not for him, except enjoining good, forbidding evil, or the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan hadith."

In another hadith: "When a servant wakes up, all the limbs humble themselves before the tongue, saying: 'Fear Allah concerning us, for we are only dependent on you. If you are upright, we are upright, and if you are crooked, we are crooked.'"

Some of the salaf used to call themselves to account for their speech, saying: "A hot day," and "a cold day."

Some of the eminent scholars were seen in a dream, and were asked about their state. He said: "I am detained because of a word I said. I said: 'How much people need rain!' and I was told: 'How do you know? I know best the interest of My servants.'"

One of the Companions once said to his slave-girl: "Bring the tablecloth, let us play with it." Then he said: "I seek Allah's forgiveness. I do not speak a word except that I restrain it and bridle it, except this word, which came out of me without a rein or a bridle," or as he said.

The easiest of the movements of the limbs is the movement of the tongue, and it is the most harmful to the servant.

The salaf and the khalaf disagreed over whether everything that is uttered is recorded, or only good and evil. There are two opinions, the more apparent of which is the first.

Some of the salaf said: "Every speech of the son of Adam is against him and not for him, except what is from Allah and what draws near to Him." Al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) used to hold his tongue and say: "This has brought me to the watering places. Speech is your captive, but when it leaves your mouth, you become its captive." And Allah is beside the tongue of every speaker: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is an observer with him, ready (to record)﴾.

There are two great afflictions of the tongue. If a servant is freed from one of them, he is not freed from the other: the affliction of speech and the affliction of silence. Each of them may be greater in sin than the other at its own time. The one who is silent about the truth is a mute devil, disobedient to Allah, a hypocrite and a flatterer, if he does not fear for himself. The one who speaks falsehood is an eloquent devil, disobedient to Allah. Most people deviate in their speech and their silence, and so they fall between these two types. The people of the middle path, who are the people of the Straight Path, restrain their tongues from falsehood and let them loose only in what will benefit them in the Hereafter. You will not see one of them say a word that is wasted without benefit, let alone one that harms him in his Hereafter.

On the Day of Resurrection, a servant may come with good deeds like mountains, and find that his tongue has demolished them all for him. And he may come with sins like mountains, and find that his tongue has demolished them through its abundant remembrance of Allah and what is connected to it.

Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Tafsir al-Qayyim*, on Surah 50, verse 37 (part 1 of 2):

God, glorified is He, combined hearing (*sam'*, revelation) and reason ('aql), and established His proof over His servants through both of them. Neither of them is ever separated from its companion. The revealed Book and the perceiving intellect are God's proof over His creation, and His Book is the greatest proof. It is the one that made known to us what our intellects could never have independently grasped. No one has any escape from it, and no one has any other refuge in place of it for something unknown that he wishes to know, a problem he wishes to resolve, or an ambiguity he wishes to clarify. Whoever turns away from it must return to it, and whoever rejects its judgment must argue against his opponent by means of it. It is, in truth, the guide to the rational paths and the certain knowledge that people need most. Whoever among those who claim to investigate and reflect rejects its judgment and dismisses its authority has been stubborn and obstinate. No one can make him understand, debate with him, or establish the truth for him. Nor can anyone say, "I am not content with its judgment, but with the judgment of reason." For whoever rejects its judgment has rejected the judgment of clear reason and opposed both the Book and reason.

Those who, from among the deficient in intellect and in understanding of revelation, claim that reason must be given precedence over revelation when they conflict, have only come to this from their ignorance of the judgment of reason and the implication of revelation. They supposed what is not rational to be rational. In reality, it is only doubts that they imagine to be clear reason, and they are not. Or they came to it from their ignorance of revelation, either by attributing to the Messenger (ﷺ) something he did not intend by his words, or by not distinguishing between what reason cannot perceive and what reason can perceive to be impossible. These are four matters that caused them to think there is a conflict between revelation and reason:

First: that the matter in question is not one of the matters of reason.
Second: that the revelation in question is not from the sound, accepted revelation.
Third: failure to understand what the speaker intended.
Fourth: failure to distinguish between what reason declares impossible and what reason does not grasp.

God, glorified is He, argues with His servants through the tongues of His messengers and prophets, concerning what He wishes to establish for them and to bind them to, by the paths closest to reason, the easiest to grasp, the least burdensome, and the most fruitful, beneficial, and valuable in outcome.

His rational proofs, which He explained in His Book, combine being both rational and revealed, clear and evident, few in premises, easy to understand, close to grasp, decisive in dispelling doubts and objections, and binding upon the stubborn and the denier. For this reason, the knowledge derived from them is more firmly rooted in hearts and more beneficial to all people.

If one who investigates surveys what is in the Book of God of the proofs He gave His servants to establish monotheism (*tawhid*), to affirm the divine attributes, to affirm the message and prophethood, to affirm the return (*ma'ad*) and the resurrection of bodies, the ways of affirming His knowledge of every hidden and manifest thing, the all-encompassing extent of His power and will, His sole possession of sovereignty and governance, and that none deserves worship but Him, he will find the matter in that regard to be as we have described: God's discourse in this regard is in the most excellent forms of argument, the most quickly reaching the hearts, the most in harmony with reason, the most distant from doubts and objections, in the most concise, clear, sweet, beautiful, and eloquent wording, and the most indicative of the intended meaning.

He said in *Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah* (*The Key to the Abode of Happiness*):

The aim is to explain how knowledge is denied to a person through these six aspects:

The first is abandoning questioning.
The second is poor attentiveness and not lending the ear.
The third is poor understanding.
The fourth is failure to memorize.
The fifth is not spreading it and not teaching it. For whoever hoards his knowledge and does not spread it or teach it, God afflicts him with forgetting it and losing it, as a recompense of the same kind as his deed. This is a matter witnessed by the senses and by experience.
The sixth is not acting upon it. For acting upon it necessitates remembering it, pondering it, observing it, and reflecting upon it. If one neglects to act upon it, he forgets it.

One of the early generation (*salaf*) said: "We used to seek help in memorizing knowledge by acting upon it."

Another of the early generation also said: "Knowledge calls out for action. If it answers, it stays; if not, it departs."

Therefore, acting upon it is among the greatest causes of its preservation and firmness, and abandoning acting upon it loses it. Nothing draws out knowledge or attracts it like action. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear God and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy and make for you a light by which you will walk﴾.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear God; and God teaches you﴾, it is not of this category. Rather, they are two independent clauses: one is imperative, namely the command to fear God, and the other is declarative, namely His saying ﴿and God teaches you﴾, meaning, "God teaches you what you fear (of His commands)." It is not an answer to the command to fear God. If it were intended as a consequence, it would have been expressed in the jussive without the conjunction *wa*, so it would have said: "Fear God, He will teach you," or "If you fear Him, He will teach you," as He said: ﴿If you fear God, He will grant you a criterion﴾. So ponder this.

(A noble principle)
If you wish to benefit from the Qur'an, gather your heart when reciting and listening to it, lend your ear, and be present as one addressed by the One who spoke it, God, glorified is He, from Him to you. For it is an address from Him to you through the tongue of His Messenger. He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is present﴾.

That is because the complete effect, when it depends upon an effective agent, a receptive locus, a condition for the effect to occur, and the absence of an obstacle that prevents it, the verse includes the explanation of all of that in the most concise and clear wording and the most indicative of the intended meaning. His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾ points to what preceded from the beginning of the surah up to this point, and this is the effective agent. His saying ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾ is the receptive locus, meaning the living heart that understands from God. As He said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an, to warn whoever is alive﴾, that is, alive in heart. His saying ﴿or gives ear﴾ means he turns his hearing toward it and attends with his sense of hearing to what is said to him, and this is the condition for being affected by speech. His saying ﴿while he is present﴾ means present of heart, attentive and not absent. Ibn Qutaybah said: "He listens to the Book of God while being present of heart and understanding, not heedless or inattentive." This points to the obstacle that prevents the effect from occurring, namely the heart's inattention and its absence from understanding what is said to it, considering it and reflecting upon it. So when the effective agent is present, which is the Qur'an, and the receptive locus, which is the living heart, and the condition is met, which is attentiveness, and the obstacle is removed, which is the heart's preoccupation and distraction from the meaning of the address and its turning toward something else, the effect occurs, which is benefiting and being reminded.

If it is said: "If the effect is only completed by the combination of these, then what is the purpose of the particle *aw* (or) in His saying ﴿or gives ear﴾, when the context requires the conjunction *wa* (and) of togetherness, not the *aw* which means one of two things?"

It is said: "This is a good question. The answer to it is that the statement came with *aw* according to the condition of the addressed person being called. Among people is one whose heart is alive and aware, of complete natural disposition (*fitrah*). When he reflects with his heart and his thought roams, his heart and intellect guide him to the truth of the Qur'an, that it is the truth, and his heart bears witness to what the Qur'an reports. So the descent of the Qur'an upon his heart is light upon the light of the natural disposition. This is the description of those about whom it was said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. And regarding them He said: ﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp within a glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. God guides to His light whom He wills﴾. This is the light of natural disposition upon the light of revelation, and this is the state of the owner of the living, aware heart."

The owner of the living heart has the fullest connection between his heart and the meanings of the Qur'an, so he finds them as if they had been written in it. He recites them from memory.

Among people is one who is not of complete readiness, aware heart, or perfect life, so he needs a witness to distinguish for him between truth and falsehood. The life of his heart has not reached the level of contemplating and reflecting upon it and understanding its meanings, so then he knows that it is the truth.

The first is the state of one who saw with his own eyes what he was called to and was informed about. The second is the state of one who knew the truth of the report and was certain of it, and said: "Its report suffices me." The second is at the station of faith (*iman*), and the first is at the station of excellence (*ihsan*). This one has reached knowledge of certainty (*'ilm al-yaqin*), and his heart has ascended from it to the rank of the eye of certainty ('*ayn al-yaqin*). With it comes the firm affirmation by which he exited disbelief and entered Islam.

The eye of certainty is of two kinds: one in this world and one in the Hereafter. What is attained in this world, its relation to the heart is like the relation of the witness to the eye. What the messengers reported of the unseen will be witnessed in the Hereafter with the eyes, and in this world with insight. So it is the eye of certainty in both stages.
