(Section)

He, exalted is He, said regarding His manifest signs: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were greater than them in strength, and they searched through the lands. Was there any escape? Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is present﴾.

People are of three kinds:

A man whose heart is dead. He is the one who has no heart, so this verse is not a reminder for him.

The second is a man who has a living, receptive heart, but he does not listen to the recited verses through which God informs about the manifest signs, either because they have not reached him, or because they have reached him but his heart is occupied with something else. He is absent of heart, not present. So he too does not attain the reminder, despite his readiness and the existence of his heart.

The third is a man of living, receptive heart. The verses are recited to him, so he turns his hearing to them, lends his ear, brings his heart present, and does not occupy it with anything other than understanding what he hears. He is present of heart, lending his ear. This category is the one that benefits from the recited and the witnessed signs.

The first is like the blind man who cannot see.
The second is like the sighted one who directs his sight elsewhere than toward what is seen. Both do not see it.
The third is like the sighted one who has fixed his gaze upon the object seen, followed it with his sight, and faced it from a middle distance, neither too far nor too near. This is the one who sees it.

Glory be to Him who made His speech a healing for what is in the breasts.

If it is said: "What is the position of *aw* in this composition, according to what you have established?"

It is said: "It has a subtle secret. We do not say that it means *wa* (and), as the literalist grammarians (*zahiriyyat al-nuhat*) say."

Know that a man may have a sharp, lucid heart, full of drawing out lessons (ʿibar) and deducing wisdoms (ḥikam). His heart impels him to remembrance and reflection (iʿtibar), so when he hears the verses they are light upon light for him. These are the most perfect of God's creation and the greatest of them in faith and insight, to the point that what the Messenger informed them of is as though witnessed by them, though they did not perceive its details and varieties. It has been said: the likeness of the state of al-Ṣiddīq (Abu Bakr) with the Prophet ﷺ is like the likeness of two men who entered a house. One of them saw its details and particulars, while the other's hand fell upon what was in the house but he did not see its details or particulars; yet he knew that there were great matters in it which his sight did not reach in their details. Then they both went out, and he asked him about what he had seen in the house. Every time he told him something, he confirmed it, because of what he had of its evidences. This is the highest rank of siddiqiyya (truthfulness). Do not deem it far-fetched that God, the Bestower (al-Mannān), might bestow such faith upon a servant, for God's bounty cannot be confined or counted.

So the possessor of this heart, when he hears the verses while there is in his heart a light of insight, is increased in light upon his light. But if the servant does not have such a heart, yet he gives ear and his heart is present and not absent, remembrance is attained for him too: ﴿But if heavy rain does not reach it, then a light drizzle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265]. The heavy rain (wābil) and the light drizzle (ṭall) apply to all deeds, their effects and their necessary consequences. The people of Paradise are foremost (sābiqūn), those brought near (muqarrabūn), and companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn), and between them lies what lies between them in degrees of preference, to the point that the pure drink of one of the two categories is made pleasant by the drink of the other category, which is blended with it in a blending. God the Exalted said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth and guides to the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Saba': 6].

Every believer sees this, but the seeing of the people of knowledge has one hue, and the seeing of others has another hue.

(Section)

God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness﴾.

So reflect upon what treasures of knowledge lie beneath these words, and how observing them opens for the servant the doors of knowledge and guidance, and how the door of knowledge is closed to him by neglecting and failing to observe them. For He, glorified be He, commanded His servants to reflect upon His verses, those recited and heard and those seen and witnessed, by which they become a reminder for whoever has a heart. For whoever lacks a heart that is aware of God does not benefit from every verse that passes over him, even if every verse passes over him. The passing of the verses over him is like the rising of the sun, the moon and the stars, and their passing over one who has no sight. When one has a heart, he is like the seeing person: when visible things pass before him, he sees them. But the possessor of a heart does not benefit from his heart except through two matters:

The first is that he be present and attentive to what is conveyed to him. If he is absent, journeying in wishes, desires and fancies, he does not benefit. When he brings it present and attentive, he benefits only by giving ear and inclining his whole self to what he is admonished with and guided to.

Here there are three matters:
The first: the soundness, health and receptivity of the heart.
The second: its presence, gathering and preventing it from wandering and scattering.
The third: giving ear, attending and turning to the remembrance. God mentioned the three matters in this verse.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "the heart" (al-qalb) here is an expression for the intellect, since it is its locus. The meaning: for whoever has an aware heart that benefits from it.

He said: al-Shiblī said: "a heart present with God, never heedless of Him for the blink of an eye."

As for His saying ﴿or gives ear﴾, its meaning is: he turns his hearing to these admonishing reports and fixes them in his hearing; that is "casting" (ilqāʾ) upon them, and from it is His saying ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾, i.e., fixed it upon you.

As for His saying ﴿while he is a witness﴾, some interpreters said: its meaning is: while he is a witness, attentive to the matter, not turning away from it, nor thinking about anything other than what he hears.

He said: Qatādah said: it is an indication of the People of the Book. It is as if He said: indeed these lessons are a reminder for one who has understanding, so ponder the matter; or for one among the People of the Book who hears them and so bears witness to their truth, because he knows them from his Book, the Torah, and the rest of the books of the Children of Israel.

He said: so (shahīd) on the first interpretation is from witnessing (mushāhadah), and on the second interpretation is from testimony (shahādah).

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning of ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾ is one whose heart is elevated to understanding. Do you not see that His saying ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ refers to those who did not listen with the listening of one who seeks understanding and guidance, so they were made like one who did not hear, as the poet said:

"Deaf to what displeases him, though hearing."

The meaning of ﴿or gives ear﴾ is listens and does not occupy his heart with anything other than what he listens to. The Arabs say: "Cast your hearing to me," i.e., listen to me.

﴿while he is a witness﴾ means his heart is with what he hears. It has been reported in the tafsir that it refers to the People of the Book who have the description of the Prophet.

So the meaning of ﴿or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ is: witnessing that the description of the Prophet is in His Book. This is what Ibn ʿAṭiyya related from Qatādah, and he mentioned that shahīd here means shāhid, i.e., one who informs.

Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf said: "for whoever has a heart" means an aware heart, because whoever's heart is not aware is as if he has no heart. "Casting the hearing" means giving ear and attending. ﴿while he is a witness﴾ means present with his acumen, because whoever's mind is not present is as if absent; or he is a believer bearing witness to its soundness and that it is revelation from God, and this is among the witnesses in His saying ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾. And from Qatādah: "while he is a witness to its truthfulness from the People of the Book, due to the existence of its description in their possession."

There is no disagreement that the intended meaning of "the heart" is the aware heart, and that the intended meaning of "casting the hearing" is his giving ear and turning to the one who admonishes and emptying his hearing for him.

They differed about "the witness" in four statements:
The first: that it is from witnessing (mushāhadah), which is presence. This is the most correct statement, and nothing other than it is fitting for the verse.
The second: that it is "witness" from testimony (shahādah), and on this there are three statements:
The first: that he is a witness to the soundness of what he has of certainty.
The second: that he is a witness among the witnesses over mankind on the Day of Resurrection.
The third: that it is a testimony from God in his possession to the soundness of the prophethood of the Messenger of God ﷺ by what he knows of the revealed books.

The correct view is the first, for His saying ﴿while he is a witness﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), and the waw in it is the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl). That is: he gave ear in this state. This requires that his being a witness be the state at the time of his giving ear, and this is from witnessing and presence. Had the intended meaning been testimony in the Hereafter or in this world, there would be no point in restricting it to the act of giving ear. For the statement would become: indeed in that is a sign for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness to what he has in the Torah, or while being a witness on the Day of Resurrection. There is no doubt that this is not the intended meaning of the verse. Furthermore, the verse is general to everyone who has a heart and gives ear, so how can its restriction to the believing People of the Book, who have testimony from their books concerning the description of the Prophet, be claimed? Also, the sūrah is Meccan, and the address in it cannot be restricted to the People of the Book, especially such an address in which the realization of the verse's content and purpose is tied to the aware heart and giving ear; so how can it be said that it is about the People of the Book?

If it is said: what is restricted to them is His saying ﴿while he is a witness﴾, this is more corrupt and more corrupt still, because the pronoun in His saying ﴿while he is a witness﴾ refers to the whole of what preceded, namely whoever has a heart or gives ear. How can it be claimed that it returns to something which at most is part of what was mentioned earlier, with no indication in the wording of it?

Also, the thing witnessed is omitted, with no indication in the wording of it. Had the intended meaning been "while he is a witness to such-and-such," the thing witnessed would have been mentioned, since nothing in the wording indicates it.

This differs from the case where it is taken as from shuhūd, which is presence, for that does not require an object witnessed, so the sentence is complete by mentioning it alone.

Also, the verse contains a division and an alternation between two categories:
The first: whoever has a heart.
The second: whoever gives ear and is present with his heart and not absent. So he is present of heart, witnessing and not absent.

This, God knows best, is the secret of using "or" (aw) rather than "and" (wa), because those among people who benefit from the verses are of two types:
The first: the one with an aware, pure heart, who is satisfied with being guided by a slight reminder, and who does not need to draw his heart in, make it present and gather it from the places of its scattering. Rather his heart is aware, pure, receptive to guidance and not averse to it. Such a one needs only the arrival of guidance to him, for the completeness of his readiness and the soundness of his nature. When guidance comes to him, his heart hastens to accept it, as though it had been written in it; he has grasped it in summary, then guidance comes with the details of what his heart had testified to in summary.
This is the state of the most perfect of creation in responding to the call of the Messengers, as was the state of al-Ṣiddīq al-Akbar, may God be pleased with him.
The second type is the one who lacks this readiness and acceptance. When guidance reaches him, he gives ear with his hearing, brings his heart present, gathers his thought upon it, and knows its soundness and goodness by his reflection and reasoning.
This is the method of most of those who respond, and for them there is the kind of striking of examples, establishing proofs, mentioning objections and answering them.
The first are those who call with wisdom (ḥikmah), and these call with fine exhortation (mawʿizah ḥasanah); these are the two types of those who respond.
As for the opponents who call to the truth, they are of two types: one type calls with disputation in the best manner; if they respond, well, otherwise there is disputation, and for these there must be argument or fighting.
Whoever reflects upon the call of the Qur'an finds it comprehensive of these categories, encompassing all of them, as the Exalted said: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and fine exhortation, and dispute with them in the best manner﴾.
So these are those called by speech. As for the people of combat, they are those whom God commanded to be fought until there is no strife and the religion is entirely God's.
As for the one who explains the verse by saying that "the one who has a heart" means the one who is independent by his nature of the science of logic, and who is supported by a holy power by which he attains the middle term quickly, so he, by the completeness of his nature, is independent of observing the conventions of logic; and that "the one who gives ear while he is a witness" means the one who lacks this power, so he needs to learn logic in order that observing it obliges him, and his attending to it, that he not deviate in his thinking — this is an interpretation which is far from the intended meaning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 50, verse 38:

(Section: On the Devil's Trickery Against This Angry Ummah)

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some discussion:

They confronted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, with statements of this kind of disbelief.

One of them said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, glorified and exalted is He, created the heavens and the earth in six days, then He rested."

This troubled the Prophet (ﷺ). So Allah, exalted is He, revealed in refutation of them:

﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ [Qaf: 38]

And consider His words that follow it: ﴿So be patient over what they say.﴾ [Qaf: 39]

The enemies of the Messenger (ﷺ) attributed to him what does not befit him and said about him what is far removed from him. So Allah, glorified and exalted is He, commanded him to be patient over their words, and to take his Lord as an example, since His enemies also said about Him what does not befit Him.
